title: Inline Styling for React Elements
summary: Explains inline styling in JSX: the style attribute takes a JavaScript object (not a string), which produces the double-curly-brace syntax. Properties are camelCased, values are strings, and the main benefit is that styles can change at runtime by updating the object.

concepts.heading: style takes an object, not a string
points: In plain HTML, style="color: red" is a string. In JSX, a string value triggers a console error saying style expects a mapping of properties to values.
The value must be a JavaScript object: { color: "red" }. Keys behave like property names (unquoted), values are usually strings, and pairs are separated by commas rather than semicolons.

Because a JSX attribute needs curly braces to hold JavaScript, and the object literal has its own braces, the result is style={{ color: "red" }}. The outer pair means 'JavaScript expression here'; the inner pair is the object itself.

concepts.heading: Property names and values
points: CSS properties written in kebab-case must be converted to camelCase as object keys: font-size becomes fontSize, background-color becomes backgroundColor.
Values are strings, including multi-part values such as "1px solid black" for border. Spaces are preserved inside the string.
(Extra) Plain numbers are allowed for many properties and React appends px (fontSize: 20 gives 20px), but unitless-capable properties such as lineHeight and opacity are left as numbers.

concepts.heading: Pulling the style into a variable
points: Move the object into a const (customStyle) declared above the component, then use style={customStyle}. This keeps the JSX readable and is the form used when the style needs to change.
The object can be changed before render, e.g. customStyle.color = "blue", and the element picks up the new value the next time it renders, with no change to the JSX itself.
This is the headline reason to use inline styles: styles driven by data such as user actions, the time of day or app state. In later lessons this combines with state so the UI restyles itself.

concepts.heading: Class-based versus inline
points: The React docs recommend classes in a stylesheet applied with className as the default approach; inline styles are the less common option reserved for dynamic values.
Inline styles cannot express pseudo-classes (:hover), media queries or keyframes, which is another reason classes stay the default. (Extra)

pitfalls: Passing a string to style raises an error in React.
Using font-size (kebab-case) as a key is a syntax error; write fontSize or quote the key.
Separating declarations with semicolons inside the object is invalid; use commas.
Forgetting to quote values such as "20px" or "1px solid black" causes a syntax error.
(Extra) Mutating a plain const object only shows up when the component re-renders; later lessons use state to trigger that properly.

gaps_and_ideas: Could be a second part of a 'Styling React' lesson. Tasks: convert a string style to an object, rename three kebab-case properties, move the style into a const, and switch its colour based on a time-of-day variable.
Interactive demo: sliders and a colour picker that edit a style object live and show both the object literal and the resulting element.
